explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, is king in Judah, and the text says their sins “…provoked Him to jealous anger more than all their fathers had done.” That's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be.

I get the thought, friend, because you'd hope each new king cleans up a little. But the text goes the other way. Under Rehoboam, Solomon's son, Judah's sins “…provoked Him to jealous anger more than all their fathers had done.” It's more, not less.

explanations.answer: About as much as their fathers
explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but the text says more than that. It doesn't say Judah matched their fathers. It says the sins they committed under King Rehoboam, Solomon's son, “…provoked Him to jealous anger more than all their fathers had done.” That's a step past the line, and it's a sad one.

I see why that one tempts you, baker, but the text says the opposite. Under King Rehoboam, Judah's worship didn't look nothing like those nations. The text says, “They imitated all the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.” Imitating them is the opposite of looking nothing like them.

That's right, baker. The text says Judah, under King Rehoboam, “…imitated all the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.” Judah copied what those nations had done. It's a sobering verse, and the text doesn't soften it.

explanations.answer: The treasures of the temple and the palace
explanations.explanation: Yep. Shishak, Egypt's king, grabbed the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. The text says he “took everything.” I think the king of Egypt came to Jerusalem with a very big bag.

That's a good guess, friend, but the text never says Rehoboam was captured. Shishak, Egypt's king, seized the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. After that, Rehoboam is still king and is making new shields (1 Kings 14:27).

explanations.answer: The young men of Jerusalem as captives
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. The text names what Shishak, Egypt's king, seized: the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. It says “He took everything, including all the gold shields that Solomon had made.” The captives answer isn't what the text gives.
Bronze it is, baker. Shishak, Egypt's king, had taken the gold shields Solomon had made, so Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place. Same job, less shine. Gold to bronze is a rough trade.
Gold is what the old shields were made of, friend. Shishak, Egypt's king, took all the gold shields that Solomon, Rehoboam's father, had made. Then King Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place.

Silver sounds like a decent step down from gold, baker, but the text says something else. After Shishak, Egypt's king, took the gold shields, King Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place. Bronze is the answer the text gives.

That's it, baker. The guards bore the shields whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, and later they returned them to the guardroom. So the shields were brought out for the king's visits and then put away. I think that's a lot of walking for a shield that isn't gold.

I see the logic, friend, since shields that used to be gold might feel like treasure. But Shishak, Egypt's king, had already cleaned out the treasures. The text says the guards returned the new bronze shields to the guardroom.
That would make a nice display, baker, but the text doesn't say it. The guards carried the shields for the king when he went into the house of the LORD. Afterward they returned them to the guardroom.

Yes, baker. The text says, “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” Jeroboam was the king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Two kings, and war between them throughout their days.

I get why you'd hope so, friend, but the text says otherwise. “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” Jeroboam was king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Throughout their days is how the text puts it.

Right, baker. The text says Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David. Rehoboam is Solomon's son, as the text says when it introduces him. The City of David is the place the text names.
Hebron is a fair guess, friend, but the text names a different place. Rehoboam was buried with his fathers in the City of David. That's the answer the text gives.
Not Bethel, baker. That's a northern town, and it's where Jeroboam put up one of his golden calves (1 Kings 12:29). Rehoboam, king of Judah, was buried with his fathers in the City of David.

explanations.answer: In all the sins of his father
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says Abijam, Rehoboam's son, “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…” He didn't pick up one or two of his father's sins. He took the whole set.

explanations.answer: Closer to the LORD than his father
explanations.explanation: Nice hope, friend, but that's not what the text says. Abijam, Rehoboam's son, “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…” The text adds that “…his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been.”

explanations.answer: Away from every idol in Judah
explanations.explanation: That's more like what Abijam's son Asa does, baker. Asa removed all the idols that his fathers had made. Abijam, Rehoboam's son, went the other direction, since the text says he “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…”

Right, baker. The text says Abijam's heart “…was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been.” David was the standard the writer measures him against. Abijam came up short.

Solomon was Abijam's grandfather, baker, since Rehoboam was Solomon's son. But the text points further back. It says Abijam's heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD “…as the heart of David his forefather had been.”

Abraham is a big name, friend, and I've grabbed the biggest name in the room before myself. The writer sets Abijam beside David instead. The text says his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God “…as the heart of David his forefather had been.”

explanations.answer: A son to succeed him and make Jerusalem strong
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says the LORD gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem “…by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong.” The lamp is a son, and Asa is that son. The text says the LORD did it for the sake of David.

explanations.answer: A prophet to speak the LORD's word to him
explanations.explanation: A prophet would be a big gift, baker, but the text doesn't say that. The lamp is explained right in the verse. The LORD gave it “…by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong.”

explanations.answer: A victory over Jeroboam king of Israel
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since there was war the whole time. But the text doesn't call a victory the lamp. The LORD gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem “…by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong.” That's a son, friend.

That's right, baker. The text says David “…had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.” The writer doesn't hide it, and he doesn't make a big speech about it either. The one exception is named plainly.

Ahimelech isn't the name in this verse, friend. The text says David had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Uriah is the one the writer names.
Not Ephron, baker. This verse names one exception in David's life, and it's the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Everything else, the text says, David followed all his days.

That would be nice, baker, but the text says it didn't end. “…there was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life.” The text adds that there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:7). The fighting kept going into the next reign.

Yes, baker. The text says, “…there was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life.” Abijam, Rehoboam's son, took the throne, but the fighting didn't change hands with it. It carried right on.
That's right, baker. The text says Asa's grandmother's name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. Remember that name, because she comes up again in this passage. Things get personal for Asa.

Michal was a real woman in Israel's story, friend. She was David's wife, called “Michal daughter of Saul” (2 Samuel 6:16). But she isn't Asa's grandmother. The text says that's Maacah daughter of Abishalom.
Achsah belongs to an older story, baker. She was Caleb's daughter, from the days of Joshua (Joshua 15:16). Asa's grandmother is someone else. The text names her Maacah daughter of Abishalom.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.” Asa was king of Judah, and after two kings who walked in sin, this is a change. I'd call it a nice change.

Not this time, friend. After Rehoboam and Abijam, Asa takes the throne of Judah, and the text says, “And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.” Two kings of sin, then a king who does right.

That's not what happened, baker. Asa, king of Judah, “…banished the male shrine prostitutes from the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.” He didn't leave them standing. He got rid of all of them.
Yes, baker. The text says Asa “…removed all the idols that his fathers had made.” That's every one of them. Asa also banished the male shrine prostitutes from the land.

explanations.answer: He removes her as queen mother
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Asa removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. I think that cost him something. It's not easy when the problem has your own family name on it.

explanations.answer: He lets her keep her place
explanations.explanation: Plenty of people would've let it slide, friend, but Asa didn't. He removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Then Asa chopped down the pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

explanations.answer: He sends her away to Egypt
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention Egypt here, baker. It says Asa removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Her job was taken from her.

I see why you'd think so after all that clean-up, baker. Asa banished the male shrine prostitutes, removed the idols and chopped down Maacah's pole (1 Kings 15:12-13). But then the text says, “The high places were not removed…” Asa got rid of a lot, just not those.
That's right, baker. The text says, “The high places were not removed…” Asa did a lot of clean-up, but this was left standing. Even good kings in the text don't finish everything.

explanations.answer: Fully devoted to the LORD all his days
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says that although the high places were not removed, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days.” The writer says it plainly and doesn't hedge. Abijam's heart, by contrast, was not as fully devoted as the heart of David.

explanations.answer: Devoted to the LORD only in his early years
explanations.explanation: That's a thoughtful guess, friend, since people do fade. But the text says Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days. It names no early years and no later years. That's the whole reign.

explanations.answer: Divided between the LORD and the idols
explanations.explanation: Not so, baker. Asa banished the male shrine prostitutes and removed the idols his fathers had made. The text says his heart “…was fully devoted to the LORD all his days.” That isn't a divided heart.
Yes, baker. Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah “…to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah.” The text pairs leaving with entering. Entering is the word.

Defending sounds close, baker, but that's not the word. Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. The word in the verse is entering.

Taxing is a fun guess, friend, and I'd be braced for a toll booth too. But the text says Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. No toll in the verse, just those two words.

Right, baker. Asa sent his servants with the silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. Asa was asking a foreign king for help. The silver and gold went along with a message.

Shishak is a name from earlier, baker. He's the king of Egypt who attacked Jerusalem and took the treasures back in Rehoboam's reign. This time Asa sent his silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Aram.
Hiram, king of Tyre, goes back to Solomon's days (1 Kings 5:1), friend. He's not the one in this story. Asa sent the silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, who ruled in Damascus.

explanations.answer: Break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Asa's message says, “Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.” The silver and gold were a gift sent along with that request. The whole ask is in that one line.

explanations.answer: Send his soldiers to guard Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's a sensible idea, friend, but Asa didn't ask for it. His message asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that Baasha would withdraw from him. Guarding Jerusalem isn't in the message.

explanations.answer: Make peace between Judah and Israel
explanations.explanation: Peace would've been something, baker, but that's not the request. Asa asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that Baasha would withdraw from him. Making peace isn't in that message.
That's not how it went, baker. The text says Ben-hadad “…listened to King Asa…” and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. Staying loyal to Baasha isn't what the text shows.

Right, baker. The text says Ben-hadad “…listened to King Asa…” and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. That's the opposite of staying loyal to Baasha. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali.

Yes, baker. The text says, “When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.” He stopped as soon as he learned of it. By then, Ben-hadad's commanders were conquering cities of Israel.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.” He stopped, and he withdrew. Then King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah.

explanations.answer: Carry off its stones and timbers
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they “…carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building.” Stones and timbers, all hauled off. With no exceptions is how the text puts it.

Finishing sounds like the natural next step, friend, but that's not what the men of Judah did. They carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. Carrying them off is the opposite of finishing.

Fire is a dramatic idea, baker, but the text doesn't say that. The men of Judah carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. They hauled it all off to use somewhere else.

Yes, baker. With those materials, King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah. The materials were the stones and timbers Baasha had used for building. Those same stones and timbers went to work on Geba and Mizpah.

explanations.answer: Builds a new palace in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: A new palace would be fancy, baker, but the text doesn't say that. King Asa used the stones and timbers to build up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah. Those were towns in his territory.

explanations.answer: Repairs the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a good thought, friend, since Asa had just brought gifts into the house of the LORD (1 Kings 15:15). But the text says something else about these stones and timbers. King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah.
That's not what the text says, baker. Asa had a long reign of forty-one years, but the text says, “In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet.” So he wasn't healthy right to the end.
That's right, baker. The text says, “In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet.” I think that's a hard note to end on, and the text just states it.
Right, baker. After Asa rested with his fathers, his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place. Asa's long reign ended and the throne passed down once more. The line of David kept going.
Abijam is a name you've seen already, friend. He was Asa's father, and he reigned before Asa (1 Kings 15:8). The son who reigned in Asa's place was Jehoshaphat.

Jehoram is a good-sounding name, baker, and I bet it's the one that jumped out at you. But here the text says Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of his father David. Then his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place. After forty-one years on the throne, Asa handed it to Jehoshaphat, not Jehoram.
